sentences.t: The DC Blox data center at 807 East 16th Street stands inside Chattanooga city limits, in Hamilton County, Tennessee, which is the reason the county's new ban does not reach it.
The entry is recorded as operating at high confidence, with no capacity, no acreage, no cost, pushback unknown and no source at all.
No megawatt figure, square footage, water figure or employment figure for the building has been published.
The county around it has just stopped taking new ones.

Weston Wamp, the Hamilton County mayor, proposed the pause in late June 2026, and on Wednesday, July 15 the county commission passed it unanimously: one year, covering new data centers in the unincorporated parts of the county.

Wamp told the meeting the point was to give the new county planning department time to write zoning rules strict enough to keep the industry out, and said: "I don't think data centers are appropriate for Hamilton County. Our land is being eaten up as it is."
The county attorney Janie Varnell said an outright ban is not open to the county in law, but that zoning restrictions should work as a deterrent.
Walker County, across the Georgia line, has a moratorium from August 9, 2026 to February 5, 2027, recorded as extended.
The pause does not touch the city.

It leaves out a small data center already approved for the former Hamilton County jail building inside Chattanooga city limits, where Urban Story Ventures, led by Jimmy White, plans a music and film studio called Jailhouse Studios with short term rentals, a rooftop helipad and an Oracle data center capped at 12,000 square feet on the bottom floor.
That project is two kilometres from this building and the only other data center site within 40 kilometres.
The power here is the Tennessee Valley Authority's, peaking at 28,930 megawatts on record.
The 1,616 megawatt Raccoon Mountain pumped storage plant is nine kilometres away, the 142 megawatt Chickamauga dam ten and the 2,278 megawatt Sequoyah nuclear station 29.

unconfirmed: Our record carries no source for this entry at all, and no reporting that mentions this building specifically was found, so its size, age, power draw and ownership are unestablished, as is any local response to it. The Local 3 and NewsChannel 9 reports on the county moratorium were read only as search summaries. A Times Free Press opinion piece argued that the moratorium only pauses what is convenient, which is the objection to a rule that stops at the city line.

sentences.t: Cielo Digital Infrastructure's Montgomery County AI Campus is a data center proposed at Clarksville, in Montgomery County, Tennessee, at 350 megawatts on 107 acres.
It would take grid power from CDE Lightband, the city utility, and nothing has been built.
The record carries the same two figures at low confidence, with no cost and no developer field filled in, and its only source is a report about a different Cielo campus, at Gaffney in South Carolina.
Directory listings repeat the 350 megawatts and the 107 acres and add nothing else.
Google is already here.

Its Clarksville data center, nine kilometres away, went on to the former Hemlock Semiconductor site after a $600 million investment the state announced on December 22, 2015, creating 70 jobs on about 1,300 acres and running entirely on renewable power under an arrangement with the Tennessee Valley Authority.
A proposed 15 megawatt Sphere 3D site is 35 kilometres off.
The generation is coal.
The 2,470 megawatt Cumberland plant is 34 kilometres away, a 173 megawatt solar farm at Russellville 43, the 116 megawatt Old Hickory dam 69 and the 1,763 megawatt Paradise plant 83.
Cedar Hill, in Robertson County, adopted a two year moratorium on June 4, 2026 running to June 4, 2028, the longest of the Tennessee measures the record carries.
Montgomery County itself has no measure on record.
Compute Atlas records local sentiment towards the Cielo campus as mixed, with opposition documented, which is not the same thing as the unknown pushback the record marks.
No cost, water figure, building count, timetable or tenant has been published for it, and low confidence is the right reading of an entry whose only source is about another state.

unconfirmed: The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable and concerns Cielo's Gaffney campus in South Carolina rather than this one; the cleanview and Tennessee economic development pages were not opened. When Cielo announced a Clarksville project, where exactly it would sit, whether it has bought land and whether any county approval has been sought are all unestablished. No official, resident or company representative is quoted, and the opposition Compute Atlas records is not attached to any named group or meeting. The Google figures date from the original state announcement in December 2015 rather than from the data center's opening.

sentences.t: The landlord for the proposed Arnold data center is the United States Air Force, which is offering 274 acres at Arnold Air Force Base, near Manchester in Coffee County, Tennessee.

The Department of the Air Force has invited industry to lease underutilised land at five bases for up to 50 years: Arnold, Edwards in California, Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in New Jersey, Davis-Monthan in Arizona and Robins in Georgia.
About 3,100 acres are on offer in all, 2,115 of them at Edwards, then 300 at Davis-Monthan, 274 at Arnold, 219 at Robins and 193 at McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst.
The terms were set in Washington.

President Trump issued orders in January and July 2025 directing the Defense Department to find sites on military installations and lease the land competitively, a qualifying project has to draw more than 100 megawatts of new load and be worth at least $500 million, responses were due by November 14, 2025 and leases were to be selected in January 2026.

Bidders also have to offer fair market value for the land, pay a one time $250,000 towards the government's administrative costs, and show three AI data center projects of more than 100 megawatts of new contracted power built in the past three years.

Robert Moriarty, the Air Force deputy assistant secretary for installations, said: "AI is transforming the modern world, and these data centers are crucial for America to remain at the forefront of innovation."

Stacie Pettyjohn, of the Center for a New American Security, said of the arrangement: "I have never heard of something like this before, where some of the public land was going to be leased to private companies to use."
The project is recorded as proposed on 274 acres with no capacity, no cost and no developer field filled in, at medium confidence, and pushback marked unknown.
There is no developer because the Air Force had not chosen one.
The counties around it have been closing their doors.

Coffee County adopted a moratorium on June 9, 2026 running a year, McMinnville one on June 3 running 18 months to December 2027, and Warren County both zoning limits on March 2, 2026 and a moratorium from June 23 running a year.
None of those touch a federal base.
This is the only data center site the record holds in Coffee County and there is no other within 40 kilometres.

The nearest generation is a 150 megawatt solar farm at Elora, 43 kilometres away, then the 106 megawatt Nickajack dam at 58 and the 1,616 megawatt Raccoon Mountain pumped storage plant at 72; the grid is the Tennessee Valley Authority's.

unconfirmed: The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable and the base's own frequently asked questions page returned HTTP 403. The page previously split Arnold's 274 acres into parcels of 122 and 152 acres; no source that could be opened carries that split, so it has been removed, and the reporting gives Arnold only as a single 274 acre offering. The July 2025 order is usually cited by its number, which the reporting read here does not give. Whether any proposal was received for Arnold, from whom, and whether a lease was signed in January 2026 are unknown. No megawatt, water or cost figure specific to Arnold has been published, and no base official, resident or county official in Tennessee is quoted.

sentences.t: The town asked for a twelve month pause and the aldermen gave it eighteen.

The Hixson data center would be a 96,000 square foot building at McMinnville in Warren County, 25 megawatts, built to carry Nvidia's GB200 NVL72 platform for high density AI work, with completion set for the first quarter of 2028.
The developer owns the site already, has signed with Bloom Energy for 30 megawatts of on site solid oxide fuel cells, and plans diesel backup generators and a 25 megawatt battery.
Its own figures are about three million gallons of water a year and 50 decibels at the nearest neighbour.
It is still looking for financing and a tenant.
An online petition against the project gathered nearly 3,000 signatures, and organisers asked for a twelve month moratorium to study the long term effects.

At a meeting on Wednesday, June 3, 2026 the McMinnville board of mayor and aldermen approved 18 months instead, barring the "acceptance, processing, and approval of applications for land use, zoning, building, site plan, or conditional use permits for data centers and high-density computing systems", and requiring studies of infrastructure, the environment, sound and utilities.
It took effect at once and can be extended.
No representative of the Hixson data center was at the meeting.
The concerns raised were water supply and energy use.
The project is recorded as proposed at 25 megawatts with no acreage, no cost and no developer field filled in, at low confidence.
Pushback had been marked unknown against a 3,000 signature petition and an 18 month moratorium passed in response to it, and now reads as organised advocacy.
Warren County separately adopted zoning limits on March 2, 2026 and its own moratorium from June 23 running a year, and Coffee County one from June 9.
This is the only data center site recorded in Warren County; the nearest generation is the 154 megawatt Center Hill dam, 42 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: The developer is not named in the report read here beyond the project itself, and our record's developer field is blank; the project's own site is hixsondc.com and the county lists it as the McMinnville Warren digital site, neither of which was opened. The two level design, the Bloom Energy fuel cells, the battery and the water and noise figures come from search summaries of the Data Center Dynamics report, which is not fetchable, and are the developer's own claims. Our record gives the address only as possibly Bybee Branch Road, and nothing confirming the location was found. No resident or alderman is quoted by name in the report read here. The Tennessee Lookout report on local officials pausing data center plans returned HTTP 403.

sentences.t: The city is trying to take the land by eminent domain to stop it being built.

DC Blox, of Georgia, planned to buy a 24 acre site at Grassmere Park in south Nashville, in Davidson County, Tennessee, for about $23 million and build a data center costing more than $700 million, next door to the Nashville Zoo.
It filed a building permit for a facility of nearly 70,000 square feet before the new rules were made.
That is the whole fight.
Under Tennessee's vested rights doctrine a developer that filed for its permits before the local rules changed can claim the right to proceed anyway, and DC Blox filed before the new zoning laws.

Councilperson Rollin Horton brought two measures, one restricting data centers near zoos, schools, parks and daycares and one imposing a moratorium, with a final reading set for July 21, 2026; Mayor Freddie O'Connell filed eminent domain legislation to buy the property, which passed first reading and could be finalised from August 3 at the earliest.
The council approved the eminent domain measure on August 4.
The zoo's petition passed 540,000 signatures, and the country singer Brad Paisley and Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor, came out against the project.

The Center for Biological Diversity and the Southern Environmental Law Center wrote to raise endangered species: clouded leopards at the zoo and Nashville crayfish in the Mill Creek tributaries nearby, warning that noise and light from the site could alter breeding patterns and might breach the Endangered Species Act.

O'Connell said DC Blox's account of meeting him and the zoo to discuss environmental safeguards was "wishful thinking," even "divorced from reality", and that the timing "would suggest an attempt to disrupt tonight's Council votes on data center legislation".
The resident Adam Nicholson said: "The toll it takes on our grid and our water supply isn't sustainable. I think this is a step in the right direction to say this industry needs to be reined in."

Rita Pfeiffer, another Nashville resident, put the other complaint: "I wonder why we are once again reactively drafting rushed policy because of public outrage instead of proactively planning for our future."
The zoo's land use attorney filed a zoning appeal to overturn the permits already approved, and the zoo rejected a memorandum of understanding the company offered.

The project is recorded as proposed with no acreage, no capacity, no cost and no developer field filled in, pushback marked confirmed with organised advocacy at high confidence, and the change.org petition and a group called Glencliff Neighbors of South Nashville attached.
The record's moratorium entry for Nashville runs from July 21, 2026 to December 1, 2026, noted as a previous moratorium and litigated.
Two other Nashville schemes sit nearby: an H5 building nine kilometres off and Fisk University's 30 megawatt Quantum Leap data center ten.
The grid is the Tennessee Valley Authority's and the nearest large plant is the 1,556 megawatt Gallatin coal station, 40 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: The WPLN report is dated July 9, 2026 and the page had taken that date as the date of a council vote; it has come out, and only the July 21 final reading and the August 3 earliest date for the eminent domain measure are given there. That report does not mention a DC Blox lawsuit against Metro Nashville, so the claim that the company has sued has come out as well. The WKRN report in our record returned HTTP 403 and the WSMV and Data Center Dynamics reports were not fetched, so the permit size, the August 4 eminent domain vote, the zoo's zoning appeal and its rejection of the memorandum are attributed to our record's source list. Sheryl Crow and Jack White were named on the page as signatories and neither appears in the report read here, so both have come out; the petition total is given variously as more than 540,000 and more than 563,000 at different dates. No megawatt or water figure has been published for the project and no DC Blox representative is quoted. Whether the eminent domain action or the zoning appeal has been decided is unknown, as is whether the moratorium survived its legal challenge.

sentences.t: H5's building at 147 Fourth Avenue in downtown Nashville, in Davidson County, Tennessee, is a carrier hotel rather than a data center campus.
The entry stands as proposed with no capacity, no acreage and no cost, at high confidence, and pushback unknown.
The record's only source is a trade report about H5 and Novacap launching a data center platform and buying three carrier hotels from 365 Data Centers.
A carrier hotel is a downtown building where networks meet, usually decades old, usually a few megawatts.
Nothing on record says what H5 proposes to do here, and proposed is an odd status for a building that was bought rather than planned.
The city around it has spent 2026 arguing about data centers.

Nashville's zoning limits on record run from July 21, 2026 to December 1, 2026, noted as following a previous moratorium and as litigated; Wilson County has a moratorium from June 23 to December 23, 2026 and Cedar Hill one running two years from June 4, 2026.
The fights are close by.
Fisk University's Quantum Leap data center is two kilometres away, the contested DC Blox site by the zoo nine, and a Compass site at Franklin 27.
The 116 megawatt Old Hickory dam is 19 kilometres off and the 1,556 megawatt Gallatin coal plant 38.
Davidson County holds three data center sites on record, and this is the only one nobody is objecting to.

unconfirmed: The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable, so no source url is listed for the sentences that rest on it and each is attributed to our record's source list. The description of a carrier hotel is general knowledge, not a finding about this building. What H5 has proposed at 147 Fourth Avenue, whether anything has been filed with Metro Nashville, the building's size and power, and whether the city's zoning limits apply to it are all unestablished. No company representative, official or resident is quoted, and no reporting on this address was found.

sentences.t: A historically Black university proposed it and its own alumni started the petition against it.

Fisk University's president Agenia Walker Clark announced a $1 billion campus plan called Quantum Leap for north Nashville, in Davidson County, Tennessee, which includes a $400 million Innovation Center of 100,000 square feet: 30,000 of academic space and a 70,000 square foot technology centre, built as a shell for a data center partner.
The site is in north Nashville, near homes and schools.
Two petitions went up against it.
One was started by Winston Wright, who graduated from Fisk in 2017, and the other by Kaylynn Mourning, who lives in north Nashville.

State Representative Justin Jones, also a 2017 Fisk graduate, held a press conference at the university gates at 12.30pm on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, calling facilities of this kind unfit for Black communities in north Nashville and saying: "Our communities are not sacrifice zones for economic greed."
The university answered the same day.

It said it understood and appreciated the community's response, that it would "never cause harm" in the neighbourhood, that the centre was "intentionally designed with sustainability, mission and community at its core", and that: "This facility will be designed to operate within the community without burdening our neighbors. That was a non-negotiable design requirement."

It said it was inviting community leaders to learn more and welcomed "open dialogue with anyone who wants to better understand the facts of this project", pointing people to the Quantum Leap website and a dedicated email address.
The entry puts the shell at 30 megawatts and the cost at $400 million, with no acreage and no developer field filled in, at medium confidence.
Pushback had been marked unknown against two petitions, a state representative's press conference and a university statement responding to all of it, and now reads as organised advocacy.
The partner has not been named, which is the missing piece: the university is building a shell for somebody else to fill.
No water figure, noise figure or timetable has been published.
An H5 building is two kilometres away and the contested DC Blox site by the zoo ten; Nashville's zoning limits run from July 21 to December 1, 2026 and are recorded as litigated.
Whether they reach a university campus, and whether Fisk's plans predate them, is not established.

unconfirmed: The 30 megawatt figure is our record's and does not appear in the report read here. The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable, and the NewsChannel 5, Inside Higher Ed, Forbes and Hoodline reports were not fetched, so the description of the site as near homes and schools, and the accounts of the wider backlash, are attributed to our record's source list. Neither petition's signature count is established. No resident who signed is quoted, and the number of lawmakers who joined Justin Jones is unknown. Whether Fisk has filed anything with Metro Nashville, and who the intended data center partner is, are unknown. The relationship between the $400 million Innovation Center and the $1 billion master plan is as the university describes it.

sentences.t: Vantage Data Centers will pay Shackelford County ten million dollars a year in place of property tax, which the county was told would lift its annual operating budget by nearly 200 per cent.

Frontier, the campus behind that payment, covers about 1,200 acres at the intersection of Highway 604 and Highway 351 in Shackelford County, west Texas, and the company has announced it as a $25 billion mega campus, which the record puts at 1,400 megawatts.
The tax abatement runs ten years.
The local paper's account of the deal is specific about what the county gets.

It lists 250 full time jobs on a $25 million annual payroll, up to 6,500 workers at peak construction, $150,000 a year to local charities for the first ten years and up to ten college scholarships a year for Shackelford County students.
Construction was to begin later in 2025 and run to 2029.

Kaitlin Monaghan, Vantage's director of public policy for North America, told the county: "We are not just developers, we are long-term operators and members of the communities where we build. We plan to be here for the long haul."

Michael Falleroni, a principal at the consulting firm Ryan LLC, made the case for the jobs: "A lot of these roles can be filled by folks with a high school diploma and/or a two-year degree. They can earn solid, family-supporting wage."
No water figure appears in that account at all.
The project is recorded as under construction at 1,400 megawatts on 1,200 acres at $25 billion, at high confidence, and pushback marked unknown.
One of the sources is headlined that Vantage has broken ground on a Texas gigawatt campus for OpenAI.
This corner of west Texas is where the largest of these have gone.

OpenAI's Stargate Shackelford, built by Oracle, is 11 kilometres away, Lancium's 1,200 megawatt Clean Campus 14, the operating 421 megawatt Stargate Abilene 23 and a Crusoe expansion for Microsoft 23.
The generation nearby is all wind: 200 megawatts at Post Oak ten kilometres off, 200 at Mesquite 11, 162 at Hackberry 27 and 340 at BMP 39.
The grid is ERCOT, which the record puts at a peak of 73,825 megawatts, and where a grid connection moratorium is recorded from August 3, 2026.

unconfirmed: The megawatts, the $25 billion and the OpenAI connection come from our record and from Vantage's own announcement and trade coverage, none of which was fetched; the Data Center Dynamics reports are not fetchable. The local report carries no capacity, no cost and no water figure, which for a campus of this size is the gap in it. No resident, county commissioner or opponent is quoted anywhere that was read, and our record marks pushback as unknown. The nature of the Texas grid connection moratorium recorded in our record from August 3, 2026, and whether it affects this campus, are not established.

sentences.t: The AIG Amarillo data center is listed as operating at 2401 South Osage Street in Amarillo, in Potter County, Texas, and the only thing behind the listing is a state environmental agency's mapping layer.
The entry gives it no capacity, no acreage and no cost, at high confidence, and marks pushback unknown.
A commercial listing describes the building at the north east corner of South Osage Street and South East 27th Avenue as a former AIG call centre and data center, available to lease.
Former is the important word.
Nothing establishes that AIG still occupies it or that it still runs as a data center, and the record's status of operating rests on a regulatory map rather than on any account of what is inside.
No megawatt figure, square footage, water figure, build date or employment figure for it has been published.
What is coming to Carson County next door is of a different order.
Fermi America's HyperGrid campus, which the record puts at 17,000 megawatts, is 26 kilometres away, and it is the only other data center site within 40 kilometres.
The 1,018 megawatt Harrington coal plant is 14 kilometres from this building and the 457 megawatt Nichols gas plant 12, with 80 megawatt wind farms at Majestic I and II at 31 and 34.
The grid is the Southwest Power Pool, peaking at 48,687 megawatts on record, and Texas has a grid connection moratorium recorded from August 3, 2026.
Duos Edge AI has separately deployed small edge data centers in the Amarillo market, and Potter County has signed a contract with an AI firm for a data center in the downtown Santa Fe building.
Neither of those is this address.

unconfirmed: The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality mapping layer our record cites was not opened, and what was found otherwise is a commercial leasing listing and directory entries, so each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. Whether the building is currently a working data center, who owns it and what its power draw is are all unestablished. There is no news reporting on it that could be found and no account of any local response, which is what would be expected for an office building of this kind.

sentences.t: At full size it would use about ten million gallons of water a day, roughly a third of everything the region uses.

Fermi America, co-founded by the former Texas governor and US energy secretary Rick Perry, is building a campus of about 5,800 acres in Carson County near the Pantex plant outside Amarillo, called Project Matador and also the Donald J. Trump Advanced Energy and Intelligence Campus, with a gas fired power plant and four nuclear reactors intended for hyperscale data centers.
The entry puts it at 17,000 megawatts on 5,769 acres, under construction, with Fermi America and Texas Tech as developers.
The water comes from the Ogallala Aquifer, which supplies part of Amarillo and most of the region's farms and ranches, and which is being drained faster than it refills.
Fermi has a 99 year lease from Texas Tech and a water deal from Amarillo's city council, both with little public consultation.
People have been turning out against it.

The Amarillo Minority Coalition organised a protest at the old Potter County courthouse, where Madison Boyle asked: "Why are we using ground water that farmers could be using for agriculture, for AI data center, where it's going to deplete a resource that's not really renewable?"
Ashlyn Major called for transparency and a public vote.

Mayor Cole Stanley said: "I don't have any comments right now but will continue to communicate to my constituents as I learn more on how this project can benefit our community while still protecting Amarillo's natural resources and water."
Fermi America did not answer interview requests; Perry, the company's vice president, has emphasised water recycling.
Kendra Seawright, who organises with a group calling itself 806 Data Center Resistance, put the demand simply: "We demand the city not sell anymore water to Fermi."

The air permit application to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality drew more than 279 public comments, most of them opposed, and another group calls itself Panhandle Taxpayers for Transparency.
The record links an action network petition headed "Our water is not for sale".
Then the money moved.

On Friday, December 12, 2025 the company's shares fell as much as 46 per cent in a day after an investment grade tenant terminated a funding agreement dated November 4 that would have provided up to $150 million of construction costs, with no capital drawn before the termination; the company had lost more than two thirds of its market value since October, without yet earning any revenue.

Fermi said it remained on track to begin delivering power in 2026, that it was still negotiating a separate lease tied to a letter of intent signed in September, and that it had opened talks with several other possible electricity customers.

The record's own sources run from an 11 gigawatt announcement, through gas turbine purchases and a Westinghouse nuclear licensing application, to a report headlined that the AI power darling implodes.
The wind farms around it are 80 and 150 megawatts; the campus as recorded is more than a hundred times the nearest of them.

unconfirmed: The capacity figures do not agree: our record says 17,000 megawatts, the trade reports describe an 11 gigawatt campus, and a separate report describes a 2.6 gigawatt gas plant for it. The ten million gallons a day and the 32 per cent of regional water use come from a Media Justice fact sheet and search summaries that were not fetched, as do the 99 year Texas Tech lease, the city water deal, the TCEQ comment count and the campaign groups; all are attributed to our record's source list. The protest is given only as a Saturday, with no date. The report on the share price fall does not name the terminating tenant or any executive. What is actually built on the site, and whether the nuclear reactors have been licensed, are unknown.
